newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain stocks dive amid regulated-price doubts.
newsitem.headline: Spain stocks dive amid regulated-price doubts.

text.p: Share prices plunged on Friday amid fears that Spain's new austerity drive might hurt profits at companies where tarrifs are government-regulated, analysts said.

"The Spanish government has been very generous up to now, but in the fight against inflation the most obvious thing to do is pull down the regulated tariffs. We've had hints about what's going to happen. It's going to get more and more competitive. Basically we're expecting greater risk," said Luis Broto, of BZW equity sales in Madrid.
The Ibex-35 index of leading stocks hit a low of 3,898.08 this morning before recovering to 3,932.30 at 1405 GMT, a loss of 21.03 points, or 0.53 percent on the day.
The index was hard hit by a report in financial daily La Gaceta de los Negocios that tariffs on telephones, electricity, gas, petrol and motorways will go towards paying the public deficit next year.
The Economy Ministry denied the report.

"The state has asked (Spanish) industry for a contribution to lower inflation as long as this does not hurt corporate results but not to transfer part of their income to cut the deficit," a ministry spokesman told Reuters.

The denial did little to soothe market fears that the new government's austerity drive had done away with years of government protection and cushy, lucrative tariff rises for state-sheltered industry.

"We do expect the regulated side of the economy not to do as well over the next few years," said Eric Rovick, head of research at AB Asesores brokerage in Madrid. "(They) are going to come under pressure."
Investors were becoming increasingly worried about the 1997 budget, which the government must present by the end of September.
The four-month-old government has pledged to cut the deficit, lower inflation, shape up and privatise many state-owned groups.
Today's share prices losses follow a sharp fall in Gas Natural's share price this week after news that gas prices will rise by much less than most stock market analysts had anticipated.
Short term, traders abroad were using this as a way to take profits, a trader said.
Analysts said a period of uncertainty for some sectors, particularly electricity firms, could last for months.
New electricity charges are not usually announced until the end of the year, and there is also key legislation pending for the sector which analysts say is another risk factor.
A recent CS First Boston research note on electricity firm Iberdrola advised caution because of "the uncertain tariff environment in Spain."

Endesa, traditionally considered the most favoured among the state-participated electricity firms, could hit 6,800 pesetas, from around 7,130 pesetas today and after a poor performance so far this year, dealers said.
Telefonica however, "is a different story. It's been holding up pretty well. Tariffs have already fallen a lot so far, so it's another case," BZW's Broto said.
Energy group Repsol meanwhile should be relatively protected, mainly because the share price has already fared badly this year. But some were not ruling out further downside.
